signals.description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. signals.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
signals.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. Spaces on Wheels : a study of what driverless cars could become once they’re more than transport. visualFeast.title: How to run a local LLM on your Mac: a step by step guide for designers, Claude prompt included
visualFeast.description: How to run a local LLM on your Mac A local model runs on your own computer. You download a file once and from then on the intelligence sits on your own machine the way Figma or Photoshop does. No account, no internet, no per-token bill, nobody able to switch it off or quietly swap it for a worse version. This guide takes you from nothing to a working model you actually use. No terminal until the last section. That part is optional. Into Design Systems + AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Examples of what you can use it for: Good to know: The results are okay, but don’t expect anything groundbreaking. Cloud models are still clearly much better at the moment. Building in Figma with nothing in the cloud: figma-cli drives Figma Desktop from your machine, and it runs against a local model. You type “add my brand colours as variables” or “create 3 button components” and it appears on the canvas. On my setup an action takes three to eight seconds plus the time Figma needs to draw it. Your design system, your file and the model all stay on the laptop, which is the difference between using AI on a client project and not being allowed to. Simple websites and prototypes: A landing page, a one page portfolio, a quick thing. The model writes the HTML and CSS, you open the file in a browser and look at it. Copywriting in your own voice: This is the one that pays for itself. The system prompt is a field in the right hand panel: a standing instruction the model reads before every single message, invisible in the chat itself. Paste ten of your own past posts in there with the instruction “write like this”. Every draft from then on starts in your voice instead of generic AI voice. Mine has explicit rules in it: no em dashes, no “leverage”, no “delve”. A local model will follow those rules. Translation: Interface strings, an email to a client in another language, subtitles. Fast, free and repeatable, so you can run a hundred of them. Transcript to draft: Record a call or a talk, feed the transcript in, get a structured draft back. This is a huge time saver in my week. Boring text surgery: Rename 200 layers to a consistent scheme, clean up a CSV, rewrite alt text for a folder of images, turn messy notes into a table. Anything you would not paste into a cloud tool: A contract, a salary conversation, an NDA’d brief, a medical letter. Whole industries cannot legally send data to a third party API. This is the only way they get to use AI at all. Working offline: Flights, trains, bad wifi. And what it is bad at: Current events. A model is trained at a point in time and has no internet of its own, so it knows nothing that happened after that day. Exact maths is the second one. And very long documents, which is a memory limit rather than a lack of intelligence. What you get and what you give up What you get Privacy: Nothing leaves your machine. Client contracts, salary discussions, an NDA’d brief, medical or legal documents: all fine, because there is no server involved. No bill per use: After the download every question is free. Run it all day and the cost is electricity. It works offline: On a plane, on a train, in a conference basement with bad wifi. Nobody can change it under you: No deprecation email, no new version that suddenly writes differently, no rate limit at the worst moment. You can point it at your own stuff: Attach a document and ask questions about it, entirely offline. What you give up A notch of quality: The best cloud models are still smarter. For most everyday work you will not notice, on hard reasoning you will. Your fans: A big model working hard heats your laptop and drains the battery. Disk space: Expect 8 to 24 GB per model. Memory pressure: The model sits in RAM the whole time it is loaded. Long documents cost extra memory on top. No web access by default: It knows nothing about today unless you give it tools. Nothing here is an either-or. Keep your cloud model subscription and let the local model take some of your routine work. This is the manual route, and it is worth doing once so you understand what is on your machine. If you would rather skip it, there is a prompt at the bottom of this post that hands the whole job to Claude. Step 1: Check what your Mac can handle This is the only technical decision in the whole guide. It comes down to memory. You need an Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or newer) on macOS 14 or later . Intel Macs are not supported. On Windows you need 16 GB RAM and a GPU with at least 4 GB VRAM ( system requirements ). First, what the B means. Gemma 4 12B is twelve billion parameters. Parameters are the internal dials the model was trained with. They are the only spec number these things really have. More dials means a better model, a bigger file and more memory. That is the whole trade you are making. The rule: the model file has to fit in your RAM with room left over for macOS and whatever else you have open. Leave roughly a third of your memory free and you will be fine. 8 GB : Gemma 3 4B, 3.3 GB download. Basic, but it runs 16 GB : Gemma 4 12B, 7.6 GB. The sweet spot for most people 24 GB : Qwen 3.6 27B, 17 GB. Close Figma while it works 32 GB : Qwen 3.6 35B, 22 GB. Best all-round, what I use 48 GB and up : the same Qwen 3.6 35B, but with the context window opened right up and a second small model loaded next to it. More memory buys you room to work, not a smarter model If you are on 16 GB, Gemma 4 12B is the one to get. It is small, writes clean prose and handles a 256K context window. If you are on 32 GB or more, Qwen 3.6 35B is the best all-round model most people can run. It is what I use every day. These are examples, not the only choice. New open models land every month. Gemma and Qwen carry this guide because they are the two families that currently sit in the size a Mac can actually run, and because I have used both. DeepSeek, Llama and plenty of others live in the same library. The names in this guide will move on. The memory maths will not, so learn that part and swap the names for whatever is current when you read it. Step 2: Install LM Studio LM Studio is a normal Mac app. It has a model browser, a chat window and a settings panel. It hides the machinery underneath. Download it, drag it to Applications, open it. That is the whole install. On Apple Silicon it runs models through Apple’s MLX, which is Apple’s own framework for running this kind of thing on the graphics chip. You do not have to do anything for that, it just means models run noticeably faster on a Mac than the numbers you see quoted for PCs. Step 3: Download your first model Click the Model Search icon, the magnifying glass over a little robot, last of the four icons in the narrow strip down the left edge. A search panel opens with a field at the top and a list of staff picks below it. Type the model name in. Pick a model and the right half of the panel fills with its details. Under Download Options the same model shows up several times over in different file sizes, with names like Q4 , Q4_K_M , Q8 and sometimes MLX . That is compression. It is the one piece of jargon worth learning. Think of an export dialog. The same picture leaves Figma as a 24 MB PNG or as a 2 MB JPEG at 80 percent and nobody in the review notices the difference. Model files work the same way. For Gemma 3 12B: the uncompressed file is 24 GB, Q8 is 13 GB, Q4 is 8.1 GB. Same model, three file sizes. The quality gap between them is far smaller than the size gap. Gemma 3 12B is just the example here. Every model on the shelf ships in the same set of sizes, so the same choice comes back every time you download one. Why 4-bit is what everyone takes: What you are short of is memory, not quality. Every gigabyte you spend on a less compressed file is a gigabyte you cannot spend on a better model. Gemma 3 12B at Q8 costs you 13 GB. For four gigabytes more you can run Qwen 3.6 27B at 4-bit instead, which is more than twice the model. That trade is why 4-bit ships as the default and why LM Studio tells you to take 4-bit or higher. MLX is not a compression level, it is Apple’s own format. Same model, built to run on the graphics chip of an Apple Silicon Mac. On a Mac, take it. Take the 4-bit version. If you see an MLX build of it, take that one. What if you have more memory than you need? On a 48 or 64 GB Mac the answer is still not a bigger file of the same model. Spend the extra memory on the three things that actually help: A longer context window. This is what runs out in real work: a sixty page PDF, a full call transcript, a long chat. Going from 32K to 256K costs memory and nothing else. A bigger model, if one exists. Today the useful local range tops out around 35B. That will change. Two models loaded at once. A small fast one for quick rewrites, a big one for the work that matters, no waiting for a swap. On 64 GB you can run the largest model in this guide at its full 256K context and still have Figma open. Download sizes are for the 4-bit versions, so a 16 GB Mac downloading Gemma 4 12B is pulling 7.6 GB. Grab a coffee. One badge worth knowing. If LM Studio shows a green Full GPU Offload Possible next to the download, the whole model fits in the memory your graphics chip can reach, which is where the speed comes from. Without that badge it still runs, just slower. Step 4: Your first conversation Go back to the chat tab, click Select a model to load at the top of the window (or press ⌘L ), pick what you downloaded and type something. The first message takes a few seconds longer because the model is being loaded into memory. Two settings worth touching, both in the model panel on the right: Context length. Everything the model can see at once: your standing instructions, the conversation so far and any document you dropped in. It is measured in tokens. 32K is roughly 24,000 words, call it a fifty page document. When it fills up the oldest part drops out of view, which is exactly why a model starts forgetting the beginning of a long chat. It eats RAM, so it usually defaults low. I run mine at 32K. If your Mac slows to a crawl, this is the first number to bring back down. Reasoning. Some models pause to think for 10 to 30 seconds before answering. That is normal, not a hang. If you find it annoying for everyday writing, switch reasoning off in the same panel. You can also drag a document into the chat and ask questions about it. That happens locally too, nothing gets uploaded. And what a token is, since the number is about to show up. Models read and write in tokens rather than words. A token is roughly three quarters of a word in English, so “design system” is two of them and something like “internationalisation” is four or five. Speed is counted in tokens per second. At 26 per second the text appears slightly faster than you can read it. Speed, from my own machine (M4 Max, Qwen 3.6 35B, 4-bit MLX, about 26 tokens per second): Short chat answer: 2 to 4 seconds A LinkedIn post: 4 to 8 seconds A newsletter with subject and body: 8 to 15 seconds A blog draft from a one hour call transcript: 60 to 120 seconds Step 5: Optional, the terminal route If you are comfortable in a terminal, Ollama does the same job with one command per model and no window to keep open. ollama run gemma4:12b downloads and starts it. Same models, less clicking. This is also where it stops being a chat window and starts being a tool. My own setup runs LM Studio as a local server. Small scripts point at it: one writes LinkedIn posts, one writes newsletters, one turns a transcript into a blog draft. Each is a text file with a system prompt in it. No subscription, no browser tab. 🤖 Or let Claude do the whole thing Everything above, done for you. This needs Claude Code, the version of Claude that can use your terminal, rather than the chat window. Paste this in and let it work: Set up a local LLM on this Mac for me. I am a designer, so explain what you are doing in plain language and do not ask me to run commands myself. Step 1: Check the machine first. How much memory it has, which chip, which macOS version. Tell me what you found. Step 2: Pick the model that fits. 8 GB: Gemma 3 4B. 16 GB: Gemma 4 12B. 24 GB: Qwen 3.6 27B. 32 GB and up: Qwen 3.6 35B. Always the 4-bit build, and the MLX build if there is one. Leave about a third of my memory free. Step 3: Install LM Studio if it is not there yet, plus its command line tool. Step 4: Download the model you picked. Tell me how big the download is before you start it. Step 5: Load it with a 32K context window and start the local server. Step 6: Prove it works. Ask it one question, show me the answer and the speed in tokens per second. Step 7: Finish with three lines. Which model I now have, how to start it again after a reboot, how to stop it when the fans get loud. If something fails, tell me what failed and what you would try next. Do not retry silently. The order matters. It checks the machine before it picks anything, so it cannot download a model that does not fit. Everything it installs is the same as above: LM Studio, one model file, nothing hidden. 🧭 A note on picking models later Model names move fast and most of what you read is out of date. Two things stay true. Check the date on any list you read, including this one. Every model above was checked on Ollama in August 2026. And ignore the headline releases. The models everyone writes about this summer are 300 billion parameters and up. They do not run on a laptop and they are not for you. The interesting work for local use is happening in the 12B to 35B range. Llama, the name most people still reach for, has not shipped anything that size in a year. 🚀 Start here Download LM Studio Model Search, look for Gemma 4 12B if you have 16 GB, Qwen 3.6 35B if you have 32 GB or more Take the 4-bit MLX version Set context length to 32K Paste ten of your own posts into the system prompt and ask it for a draft If you get stuck on any of the five, the Into Design Systems Slack is the fastest place to ask. Happy agentic coding! Sil Bormüller Into Design Systems + AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

visualFeast.title: Designer Portraits: Susan Kare ⌘ The woman who gave the computer a face
visualFeast.description: Good design is not about what medium you are working in. It’s about thinking hard about what you want to do and what you have to work with before you start. — SK Susan Kare joined Apple in 1982 as the sole creator of screen graphics in the Macintosh group. As the designer “ who gave the Macintosh a smile ” she is best known for developing the distinctive icons, typefaces, and other pixel elements that gave the Macintosh its characteristic look and feel. A sculptor picks up graph paper In 1982, Susan Kare was living in the Bay Area, welding a life-size razorback hog for a museum in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Her father, Morley Richard Kare, had founded the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, spending his career studying taste and smell. His daughter had a PhD from NYU, a background in sculpture and fine art, and zero experience with computers. Then Andy Hertzfeld called. Hertzfeld and Kare had known each other since they were fourteen, classmates at Harriton High School outside Philadelphia. He was now the lead software architect on a secret project at Apple: the Macintosh. He needed someone to design the icons and typefaces for its screen. He told her if she got some graph paper, she could make small images. Kare went to the University Art supply store in Palo Alto and bought a $2.50 sketchbook. That sketchbook now sits in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Susan Kare. Apple Macintosh OS icon sketchbook. 1982 — MoMa She went to the Palo Alto public library, checked out every book she could find on typography, and brought them to the interview to prove she knew something about type. “I went into it totally green” she said later. Apple offered her a fixed-length contract to design fonts and icons. In January 1983, she started working at Apple. Her business card read “Macintosh Artist.” Susan Kare, Apple's “Macintosh Artist” relaxes at her desk in 1984. Photographer: Norman Seeff 1,024 squares The Macintosh used a bit-mapped display. The display controlled every pixel on screen. Kare’s canvas was a 32-by-32 pixel grid. 1,024 squares to communicate a single idea. She understood the constraint immediately. “Bitmap graphics are like mosaics and needlepoint and other pseudo-digital art forms, all of which I had practiced before going to Apple,” she said. “I didn’t have any computer experience, but I had experience in graphic design.” No icon editor existed when she started. She learned to calculate the hex equivalent of her pixel drawings so Hertzfeld could keyboard them into the prototype. He built her a proper editor that generated hex values under the icons. Eventually she used MacPaint itself to create icons. A MacPaint screenshot featuring Kare’s artistry, 1983. Notice the icon menu at left and the Chicago system font used for the pull-down menus. Some icons already existed from the Lisa, Apple’s earlier computer. The arrow cursor. The document with a folded corner. The trash can. The Lisa’s interface was functional but clinical, icons designed by engineers to label functions, not to invite use. It also used non-square pixels, so every element needed reworking for the Mac’s display. Kare refined the trash can. She created the application icon, a hand holding a pencil against a diamond shape, to distinguish apps from documents. She designed the Happy Mac, the smiling face that greeted users at startup. She designed the ticking bomb that appeared during system failures. For the copy function, she tried drawing a photocopier. Then she drew a cat looking in a mirror. Copy cat. She scrapped it because it wouldn’t translate internationally. The lasso, the paint bucket, the paintbrush. Each icon went through rounds of sketching on graph paper before touching a screen. Her process was the same as any visual designer working in any medium in any century. Pencil, paper, iteration. The screen was just the final surface. Kare's Happy Macintosh icon appeared at startup, greeting users with a smile to let them know everything was okay. She designed warmth into a machine. Fonts in 9 by 7 dots Most digital typefaces in 1983 were monospaced. Every character occupied the same width. Kare wanted proportional fonts, letters that breathed according to their natural shape. Each letter had to fit in a grid of 9 by 7 dots. The bold system font started as “Elefont.” It became Chicago, the typeface that would appear on the Macintosh and later the iPod for over twenty years. Kare and Hertzfeld named the early fonts after commuter train stops on Philadelphia’s Main Line: Overbrook, Merion, Ardmore, Rosemont, Paoli. Steve Jobs told them the names were too parochial. He wanted world-class cities. The fonts became New York, Geneva, London, Toronto, Venice. One font, Ransom, looked like cutout letters from a kidnapper’s note. Jobs renamed it San Francisco. Another, Cairo, featured tiny pictograms: a palm tree, a crescent moon, a skateboard. Decades before Apple introduced emoji, Kare had already drawn proto-emojis into a font. The command key and the Swedish campground ⌘ Every keyboard needs a modifier key. The Mac team struggled to find the right symbol for theirs. Kare found the answer in Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook, a reference she kept at her desk at Apple. The symbol marked interesting features on Swedish campgrounds. It was abstract enough to work as a keyboard glyph, meaningful enough to carry intention. It became ⌘, one of the most recognized symbols in computing. The pirate flag Steve Jobs liked to tell the Mac team: “ It’s better to be a pirate than join the navy. ” When the team moved into a new building, Bandley 3 , programmer Steve Capps wanted a flag. He asked Kare to design one. She drew a Jolly Roger with the eyepatch replaced by Apple’s rainbow logo. They flew it over the entrance. It stayed there for over a year. At one point, the Lisa team stole it. In 2016, Apple flew the flag again to mark the company’s 40th anniversary. This wallpape r is a nod to the Jolly Roger that flew over Bandley 3 in 1983, the building the Mac team worked in as they put the finishing touches on the Macintosh. Apple recently flew a recreation of the original 1983 flag in 2016 , when it celebrated its 40th anniversary on April 1st, shortly before moving its HQ from Infinite Loop to Apple Park. And the flag is still available on Susan Kare's website . After the Mac The Macintosh shipped in January 1984. The entire visual language Kare created came from roughly one year of work. When Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985, Kare followed him to NeXT as creative director. She was one of the company’s first ten employees. At NeXT, she connected Jobs with one of her design heroes. Kare was a devoted Paul Rand fan. She introduced Jobs to Rand’s books, and together they hired Rand to design the NeXT logo. Kare and David Kelley visited Rand at his studio. Rand, then in his seventies, told them: “I’ve been doing this for fifty-five years, and I know what you should do.” Susan Kare, center, was a creative director at NeXT, and she left with Jobs after his ouster at Apple. Kim Jenkins, right, was a key member of the NeXT marketing team. Kare founded her own studio, Susan Kare LLP, in 1989. Over the next three decades, she designed interface elements for Microsoft, Oracle, Facebook, IBM, and Sony Pictures. She designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. In 2003, she served on the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, designing coins for the United States Mint. In 2015, she joined Pinterest as product design lead. In 2018, AIGA awarded her the AIGA Medal, one of the profession’s highest honors. Kare designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. The proof of concept The Museum of Modern Art calls Kare “a pioneering and influential computer iconographer.” The label misses the point. She made the Macintosh feel human and had never touched a computer before Apple hired her. She came from sculpture, fine art, mosaics, needlepoint. She treated the pixel grid the same way she treated any design surface: as a constraint that shapes the work. “I hoped to help counter the stereotypical image of computers as cold and intimidating,” Kare said. Someone with a $2.50 sketchbook and a sculptor’s eye decided that the visual language of technology should borrow from the one humans already knew. That turned out to be enough. “I still spend my days turning dots on and off.” Today, Kare is working as a design architect at Niantic Labs and still runs her own studio in San Francisco. She sells limited-edition signed prints of her icon work, collaborates with brands like Ledger on pixel art for hardware , and her original 1982 sketchbooks remain on display at MoMA. Needlepoint to Ledger Nano™: A Conversation with Susan Kare Apple turns 50 this year. ( 50 years of thinking different. ) Researching Susan Kare felt like walking back to where it all started; reading about how she approached design problems, how she collaborated, how she used constraints to shape the work. They built the foundations of how we use computers today. They had constraints on their screens but none in their minds. I hope you enjoyed reading this one. Designer Portraits is an ongoing series about the great minds that inspire us. You can also read about Dieter Rams and Corita Kent . More portraits are on the way, follow to get notified. visualFeast.title: #299 | finalmente podemos medir as redes sociais no Google
visualFeast.description: Oi, gente 👋 Essa semana eu fiquei com uma sensação muito clara: trabalhar com redes sociais é cada vez menos para amadores - o fazedor de post, sabe? Novas camadas foram sendo adicionadas: busca, IA, distribuição mais complexa, novas métricas, novas análises, novas possibilidades. As notícias desta edição reforçam essa ideia. TL;DR Resumo do resumo das principais notícias da semana 🧠 Google Search Console agora mostra dados das redes sociais: pela primeira vez, profissionais de social media conseguem medir como seus conteúdos circulam na Busca do Google. 🧠 Instagram pode cobrar pelo uso de IA: Mosseri confirmou que recursos avançados devem ganhar uma versão paga. 🧠 TikTok aperta o cerco ao spam de IA: plataforma passa a mirar contas que publicam conteúdo sintético em massa. 🧠 Europa questiona o “design viciante” da Meta: Facebook e Instagram podem ser obrigados a rever recursos como rolagem infinita, autoplay e notificações. 🧠 IA ganha espaço na escolha de marcas: novas pesquisas mostram que consumidores estão usando cada vez mais IA para pesquisar produtos e decidir o que comprar. MANDA NEWS Links e novidades mais relevantes da semana. Isso é GIGANTE: o Google Search Console agora mostra como posts do Instagram, TikTok, X e YouTube performam na Busca e no Discover. O que muda no trabalho de social media com os novos dados do Google Search Console? Spoilier: muda tudo. Rosto sorridente rachado, picles e farol: conheça os novos emojis do iPhone 2027. Eu amo. Cada novo emoji abre novas possibilidades de comunicação pra gente. Essa semana rolou um bafafá sobre a fonte anti-IA, que só os humanos conseguem ler . Mas já foi testado e comprovado que as IAs conseguem ler, sim. Leia a thread abaixo do comentário do usuário SeriouslyYoutube. Autoridades britânicas propõem o apagão das redes sociais para adolescentes durante a noite. União Europeia exige que Meta mude o ‘design viciante’ do Facebook e do Instagram e é importante a gente acompanhar o caso. 🧠 Estão questionando diretamente o modelo que sustenta as principais métricas das redes sociais. Caso a Meta seja obrigada a criar pausas reais ou mudar seus sistemas de recomendação, alcance, retenção e comportamento de consumo devem mudar também. MANDA DADOS McKinsey analisa a jornada de consumo da Gen Z: As redes sociais são a fonte mais importante para a Gen Z tanto na descoberta de marcas quanto na compra. Influenciadores viraram fonte de informação sobre saúde. Pew analisa como jovens consomem conteúdo de saúde . Perigoso demais, vixe. Alô Mari Kruguer! Podcast em áudio e vídeo gera comportamentos diferentes. Nielsen compara quem escuta e quem assiste a podcasts . Ipsos investiga o uso de IA nas compras . Ela já já participa da consideração, mas ainda não conquistou confiança suficiente para assumir a decisão. BCG mede a influência da IA sobre as decisões. O número de pessoas que usa a ferramenta pra pesquisas marcas e serviços segue crescendo. 🧠 O marketing passa a trabalhar com dois caminhos de influência: um voltado à atenção humana e outro à avaliação feita por sistemas. trabalho cada vez mais complexo, e cada vez menos amador Artigo: Evite que a IA prejudique sua marc a . Harvard Business Review alerta para o desgaste acumulado pela automação Dados próprios aumentam as chances de citação pela IA. A Similarweb defende que levantamentos, pesquisas e números exclusivos dão aos sistemas de IA um motivo concreto para citar a fonte original. 🧠 Dados internos podem virar conteúdo de autoridade. Mas precisam ser publicados com número, metodologia, amostra, período e fonte claramente visíveis, e não enterrados em um PDF impossível de encontrar. MANDA DICAS Hootsuite atualiza guia de mensuração de ROI nas redes sociais. Sprout Social ensina a avaliar se vale entrar no Bluesky e como criar estratégias pra lá. Estratégia de marketing com micro-influenciadore s: como encontrar, fazer parceria e medir pequenos criadores, via Later. Como as principais marcas estão ativando criadores no TikTok para impulsionar resultados reais de negócios, via Later. Agora, as novidades de cada rede. INSTAGRAM Adam Mosseri diz que creators humanos ficarão mais valiosos com a enxurrada de IA. Ele argumentou que, quanto mais conteúdo sintético circular, maior será o valor de perspectivas humanas. Instagram prepara cobrança pelo uso de I A. Mosseri confirmou que futuras ferramentas de IA do Instagram deverão ter limites de uso gratuito e opções pagas. Instagram Reels adiciona mais traduções de IA em japonês, coreano, francês, alemão e italiano Instagram começa a alertar responsáveis sobre conversas preocupantes com a Meta AI FACEBOOK/META Recuou : Dois dias depois de liberar um recurso que permitia citar contas públicas do Instagram e usar seus conteúdos em imagens geradas por IA, a Meta tirou a função do ar. Meta adiciona novas métricas para acompanhar o desempenho dos chatbots THREADS O Threads agora permite curtidas privadas , onde apenas você e a pessoa que postou poderão ver que você curtiu a postagem dela. Threads adiciona tags para posts da comunidade TELEGRAM Adorei! O Telegram lançou um e ditor para textos com até 32.768 caracteres , títulos, tabelas, listas, imagens e vídeos incorporados. A atualização também permite reunir diferentes canais, grupos e bots dentro de uma mesma Comunidade. LINKED IN O LinkedIn compartihou dicas para creators e marcas: Publique de 2 a 3 vezes por semana Comece pela informação mais importante Estruture o post como pergunta e resposta Mantenha os posts entre 200 e 300 palavras Compartilhe insights atuais, perguntas que estimulem conversas ou resuma conteúdos mais longos Publique uma combinação de posts e artigos Como o algoritmo do LinkedIn funciona em 2026 , via Hootsuite. TIKTOK Madonna bate recorde de audiência em live no TikTok. Foram mais de 2,1 milhões de espectadores simultâneos. TikTok aperta o cerco ao spam de IA. Empresa vai testar sistemas para identificar contas dedicadas a publicar grandes volumes de conteúdo gerado por IA, e lança medidas de alfabetização . Vídeos gerados por IA estão sendo usados em escala para vender produtos no TikTok Shop, inclusive com avatares fazendo demonstrações (que nunca aconteceram, né?). Algumas marcas já começaram a proibir esse tipo de conteúdo. visualFeast.description: nas edições anteriores #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 A essa altura você já sabe que a Bits to Brands virou uma revista impressa . Duas, na verdade, considerando que estamos na segunda edição. Já somos praticamente uma banca. O que você talvez não saiba é que este processo criativo começou lá em 2014, quando a gente visualizou uma revista impressa que viria com um boné, feita para ser a companhia ideal para o verão de 2025. (Por isso a garota da capa estava sentada em uma cadeira de praia lendo uma revista, que dentro tinha uma página só de palavras cruzadas e vinha com um cartão postal retratando um dia de praia…) Ou seja: não basta selecionar os artigos, ordenar e diagramar de forma que faça sentido e pensar o projeto gráfico - toda revista precisa ter um tema. _ Na sua segunda edição, em 2026, o escolhido foi Bora de Brasil . Uma das grandes tendências do ano, e um tema de grande interesse por aqui - das pesquisas traduzindo a nossa cultura à possibilidade de contar mais histórias de marcas brasileiras. Imagina não ser brasileiro e não reparar no rodinho de pia? A celebração da brasilidade foi o norte para a capa, o título, as cores, a curadoria de artigos e, claro, para a experiência memorável que a gente quer que a revista seja. Aqui a gente não coloca impresso no mundo para ir parar no fundo da gaveta. Ou é para guardar, ou é para expor, ou é para interagir. Ou quem sabe até todas as anteriores. É por isso que, dessa vez, ela tem uma lombada quadrada (fica melhor na estante) , tem uma página que vira pôster (um lembrete para a sua área de trabalho) e tem um álbum de figurinhas. _ Brasilidade + impresso + offline + Copa do Mundo. A cada quatro anos essas referências se encontram na sensação de completar, uma de cada vez, dezenas de páginas de um álbum. As figurinhas, por sua vez, trazem imagens conhecidas, reconhecidas, algumas até icônicas, que representam o melhor do país naquela modalidade. A nossa modalidade é o marketing. A nossa seleção, portanto, é composta de ações de marcas que destacam o melhor da criatividade brasileira nas últimas décadas. Fiquem agora com a nossa Seleção, na certeza de que ela deixou grandes destaques de fora. Porém com a esperança de que isso gere bons debates e trocas. _ Em 2013, a Kombi contava em primeira pessoa as histórias reais que as pessoas enviaram para celebrar a sua despedida. Em 1998, a Johnson’s Baby reforçava a sua linha de shampoos infantis, e oferecia a trilha sonora para milhões de banhos de bebês dali em diante. Em 2019, o McDonald’s deixava de lado a consistência em nome do seu real significado (e grafia) para o público brasileiro. Em 1997, dois pequenos esquimós transformavam Danoninho em sorvetinho, e a gente ganhava uma frase para repetir por décadas. Em 2025, a Red Bull transformava um edifício icônico de Porto Alegre em rampa para um dos maiores skatistas do Brasil. Em 2011, alguns pôneis cantavam em volta de um carro Nissan , em um dos virais mais marcantes do início das redes sociais. Em 2020, a Netflix esgotava em algumas horas uma edição especial impressa do seu universo de conteúdo. Em 1991, uma série de conteúdos transformava uma marca em adjetivo e fazia muita gente se questionar se qualquer coisa era ou não era “assim uma Brastemp ”... Em 2025, o Canva colocou a Xuxa em um dos seus figurinos icônicos para lançar uma linha de produtos e uma campanha especial “para adultinhos”. _ Além de uma Seleção de Campanhas, a Revista Bits to Brands tem 50 páginas de conteúdo e ilustrações. Ela é a materialização da nossa identidade visual e conteúdo, e também daquilo que a gente acredita: o poder das palavras, a conexão para além das telas e o valor que as coisas ganham quando passam a fazer parte da vida real de alguém. Para viabilizar o seu envio para diferentes cantos do Brasil, estamos fazendo uma tiragem especial em forma de produto social. Você pode garantir a sua pelo valor de R$ 79,90 - e todo o lucro desta ação será destinado a uma ONG de incentivo à leitura no Brasil. Esperamos que seja uma boa leitura, uma ótima surpresa e algo significativo e duradouro como só o impresso é capaz de se tornar. Sem mais delongas: EU QUERO UMA REVISTA (é só clicar no botão - enquanto durar o estoque) para inspirar, com O Boticário #publi ✨ A nova linha Nativa SPA Ameixa Intensa foi anunciada com uma mescla de conteúdo orgânico, influenciadores e até ameixas gigantes. E O Boticário mostrou que uma boa estratégia de comunicação acontece entre o online e o offline, agregando ao entretenimento ao invés de interrompê-lo. Durante a novela Quem Ama Cuida, a marca foi inserida em meio a dois personagens que representam o seu principal atributo: intensidade. Na cena, amostras do novo hidratante são usadas e mencionadas de forma sutil. Só no break comercial que a mensagem se completa: dobro de ameixa, dobro de amostras nas lojas. E o link com oferta vai para as redes sociais minutos depois. Ou seja: quando cada canal cumpre o seu papel, a conexão emocional acontece, o produto se faz presente e a promoção aparece na hora certa. para ler com calma 📄 As marcas que souberam aproveitar a trend dos anos 80 Tudo que a Apple lançou na semana passada A última edição da Revista Gama, sobre memória “Quando você decide que quer filmar ou tirar foto, sua atenção está se voltando a quê? visualFeast.title: #303 | Marcas multiespécie
visualFeast.description: nas edições anteriores #301 | O legado da Copa do Mundo 2026 #302 | Os oráculos da timeline tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Segundo o estudo Tendências Brasil 2026, de Globo Gente: Pela primeira vez, casais com filhos são menos da metade das famílias do país; Lares unipessoais, casais com pets e uniões homoafetivas cresceram vertiginosamente; O número de pessoas que moram sozinhas triplicou de 2000 para 2022. _ É neste contexto que os animais de estimação têm ganhado status (e padrão de vida) de filhos em muitas casas brasileiras. Plano de saúde, guarda-roupas para todas as estações do ano, festas de aniversário, creches e escolas, entretenimento… Em uma economia que que movimenta um estimado de R$ 77 bilhões por ano. Quando novas configurações de família são cada vez mais “multiespécie”, esses códigos passam a fazer parte da comunicação de todo tipo de categoria. Todo mundo percebeu que falar com “pais de pet” é estratégico na busca pela atenção, cada vez mais escassa, e da conexão emocional, cada vez mais dispersa. O fator “fofo” é capaz de reter as pessoas por mais tempo, enquanto gera uma reação imediata - curtir, comentar, compartilhar e, claro, comprar. Segundo dados da Buzzmonitor, o aumento no engajamento com publicações que contém pets é de 16%. É por essas e outras que temos visto pets em todos os lugares. De montadoras de carro a fast-food (sim). Sendo público-alvo de novos produtos, influenciadores das suas causas ou apenas “bichinhos propaganda”. O movimento que impulsionou o crescimento de diversas empresas do segmento pet, agora atinge todas as que sabem aproveitá-lo. Marcas que estão se tornando multiespécie. _ O Grupo Boticário levou a sua experiência em perfumaria e desenvolvimento de produtos para uma marca dedicada a deixar a rotina com cães e gatos mais cheirosa. A Stanley lançou o Pet Bowl, feito do mesmo material dos seus produtos que retém temperaturas, para manter a água dos bichinhos gelada e evitar o uso de plástico no seu dia a dia. A Rimowa agora também tem a Pet Carrier Bag, uma bolsa para transporte de animais até 8kg que, além do cuidado no conforto e design, é feita para se acoplar às malas da marca. Até o McDonald’s está pensando no bem-estar desses membros da família. Não lanches especiais (ainda), mas com uma embalagem lançada em Singapura - a Happy Meow Bag é um brinquedo para gatos inspirado nos pacotes do restaurante. _ E talvez o maior sinal das mudanças em como representamos “família” e a inclusão dos pets na estratégia das mais diversas marcas, esteja no segmento de carros. Houve um tempo em que falar de SUVs era sinônimo de imagens de carros grandes com crianças no banco de trás e muitas malas indo pegar a estrada. Hoje, quem está sendo transportado é o cachorro. Ano passado, para lançar o novo modelo da Tracker, a Chevrolet trouxe o vira-lata caramelo como protagonista da sua campanha. Além do filme publicitário, aproveitou o hype do filme Caramelo, na Netflix, para ações em redes sociais. E essa semana mesmo, a Peugeot lançou o E-5008 Dog Edition, com funcionalidades e acessórios focados no conforto dos pets. _ Basicamente, depois de criar uma indústria inteira em torno de si, os animais de estimação agora estão conquistando espaço em marcas de todos os segmentos. Pets atraem o olhar, inspiram emoção e tornam qualquer comunicação mais memorável. Mas a sua presença é mais do que um atalho no jogo da atenção. Ela é reflexo de um novo contexto social e uma nova ideia de família. Num presente que deixa isso cada vez mais evidente, e um futuro que não mostra qualquer sinal de que isso mude. E nenhuma marca quer ficar no passado. para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Em meio a tantas marcas buscando rejuvenescer, usando inclusive a nostalgia pra atrair os mais jovens, o Burger King faz um aceno claro aos “boomers” - até no nome. O combo “Boomer King”, lançado na França, convida as pessoas que cresceram entre os anos 80 e 90 a revisitarem a sua juventude. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 Em todos esses anos de Bits to Brands, os livros são presença constante. Entre recomendações ora semanais aqui, ora ocasionais na timeline; e uma curadoria individual e também colaborativa, centenas de títulos já passaram por aqui. Aproveitamos as novas features da Amazon para organizar a nossa biblioteca em listas com links diretos. Só de marketing e branding são vinte. acesse a nossa nova biblioteca _ Falando em livros, na última semana teve Festival Literário em Paraty. Além da autora mais vendida do evento, Socorro Acioli ofereceu o que é provavelmente um dos melhores depoimentos sobre como reagir a críticas. _ Em parceira com a Porto Rocha, o Tinder foi descobrir se é possível “ser um aplicativo de relacionamentos que não tenta conversar com todo mundo, mas ainda passar a sensação de que é para todo mundo”. graphicDesign.title: Creativity in the Age of AI
graphicDesign.description: A few years before they closed, Space10 made a short film called Creativity in the Age of AI . It runs through the history of creative tools and asks what AI changes about the act of making. I keep coming back to this film these days. So let’s explore the studio behind it and explain how they pushed the boundaries of creativity in the age of AI. Located in Copenhagen’s Meatpacking District, the SPACE10 office is where the community, ideas, and explorations intersected. A studio that built by asking better questions Space10 was IKEA’s research and design lab in Copenhagen. It started in 2014, out of a project between IKEA and a Danish design collective called ArtRebels who had designed a furniture line for the retailer. When then-CEO Torbjörn Lööf called them in for a follow-up, they could have proposed another product line. But they proposed something else, as rebels do. Instead of just creating a better future for IKEA, our starting point was asking how IKEA could help create a better future for the world,” Simon Caspersen told Fast Company in 2015 . “Let’s get rid of the whole client-agency model, have IKEA pay the basic fees and costs of running a space, and then devote ourselves to looking 10 or 20 years down the pipeline. That arrangement is what made the work possible. A small team with a long horizon, free of campaigns and quarterly deliverables, working on questions that took years to answer. So they took strange ones. What if hotdogs had no meat. What if homes shipped flat and assembled in a day. What if a village block was the unit of urban design instead of the apartment. The output looked like prototypes and films and exhibitions. The real product was a way of thinking about the future that didn’t sound like a press release. How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Products of Place: Localised Design with AI I was envy of it. I still am to be honest. As a solo designer, you read about a place like that and you want to be in the room with curious people working on real stuff, tinkering at the highest level. Sadly they closed shop in 2023. But the highlights are still up. Go get lost in them. They are very inspiring projects. How they used AI Most teams now use AI to ship faster. Space10 used it to think further. They used AI to shorten the distance between an idea and a prototype they could look at and discuss about. The argument is still human. The making is partly machine. An emerging type of collaboration. DOC put the question well in their piece on the studio: When we consider the utility of AI in creativity as a feature that helps us create meaning instead of consuming content, it provides a means for us to frame how we build tools that act as collaborative partners in creative work and stimulate our creative action. So, when building creative tools with this in mind, what should the actual interaction design between humans and AI look like? — Collected Consciousness, DOC That’s the part most product teams skip. The question we should be asking is what the interaction looks like when a person and a model are working on the same thing at the same time. Space10 treated that as a design problem. The result is a studio that used AI to go deeper into questions about food, shelter, cities, and loneliness. They handed over some of the iteration and kept the question. Bee Home is a free and open-sourced design, pioneering a new era of democratic design for IKEA. The fears are old We’ve been here before. People were hostile to the camera. They were hostile to the automobile, to recorded music, to the personal computer. Painters thought photography would end painting. It ended a particular kind of portrait commission and freed painting to do something else. The fears around AI with those. Some of it is about jobs. Some is about craft. Some is about consent. Artists’ work became training data without their permission. Styles that took twenty years to develop are a prompt away. That’s a property question we still haven’t answered. The rest of the resistance follows the usual shape. A new tool changes who gets to make things, and the speed it brings starts to feel like the point. I wrote about this in Efficiency over Craftsmanship : the more design optimizes for output, the more the work drifts toward the average. AI is the strongest accelerant we’ve had. The risk is the same as before. We mistake faster for better, ship more of the average, and stop noticing what’s missing. Space10’s film tells a different use of the same tool: keep the craft, let the machine carry some of the iteration. The value of most essays we write over a lifetime sits in the effort of writing them. The thinking happens in the friction. If we hand the friction to a model, we get the essay and lose the thinking. If we hand the iteration to a model and keep the question, we get more thinking, faster. Space10’s film is an argument for the second one. Made by a team that built that way for nine years before it closed. Worth watching, and worth borrowing from. — Thanks for reading. Always good to hear what you think. Comments open. References The film Creativity in the Age of AI , Space10, directed by Joss Fong and Áron Filkey: youtube.com/watch?v=y7g-nRooZr8 Space10 Studio: space10.com Highlights of nine years of work: space10.com/highlights Inside Ikea’s Innovation Lab for the Future of Home Design, Fast Company , 2015: fastcompany.com/3053873 Selected Space10 projects worth a look Products of Place: Localised Design with AI - How can AI assist designers to make more sustainable products using abundant local materials? Tomorrow’s Meatball : Visualising the future of food, including the dogless hotdog. Future Food Today : a Space10 cookbook of recipes built around alternative ingredients. The Urban Village Project : a proposal for shared, modular living at the block scale, with EFFEKT Architects. SolarVille : a miniature neighborhood prototype running on solar microgrids and peer-to-peer energy trading. Everyday Experiments : short films exploring how spatial computing and AI could reshape the home. Bee Home : open-source, downloadable beehive designs. Spaces on Wheels : a study of what driverless cars could become once they’re more than transport. People Joss Fong, video journalist on science and tech, formerly of Vox, now co-founder of Howtown: joss-fong.com Áron Filkey, art director and visual artist working across photo, motion, and set design: aronfilkey.com Simon Caspersen, co-founder of Space10 and ArtRebels. Torbjörn Lööf, then-CEO of IKEA when Space10 was founded. ArtRebels, the Danish design collective behind Space10’s original concept: artrebels.com Further reading Collected Consciousness , DOC: doc.cc/articles/consciousness Efficiency over Craftsmanship , UX Collective: uxdesign.cc/efficiency-over-craftsmanship

graphicDesign.title: How to run a local LLM on your Mac: a step by step guide for designers, Claude prompt included
graphicDesign.description: How to run a local LLM on your Mac A local model runs on your own computer. You download a file once and from then on the intelligence sits on your own machine the way Figma or Photoshop does. No account, no internet, no per-token bill, nobody able to switch it off or quietly swap it for a worse version. This guide takes you from nothing to a working model you actually use. No terminal until the last section. That part is optional. Into Design Systems + AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber. Examples of what you can use it for: Good to know: The results are okay, but don’t expect anything groundbreaking. Cloud models are still clearly much better at the moment. Building in Figma with nothing in the cloud: figma-cli drives Figma Desktop from your machine, and it runs against a local model. You type “add my brand colours as variables” or “create 3 button components” and it appears on the canvas. On my setup an action takes three to eight seconds plus the time Figma needs to draw it. Your design system, your file and the model all stay on the laptop, which is the difference between using AI on a client project and not being allowed to. Simple websites and prototypes: A landing page, a one page portfolio, a quick thing. The model writes the HTML and CSS, you open the file in a browser and look at it. Copywriting in your own voice: This is the one that pays for itself. The system prompt is a field in the right hand panel: a standing instruction the model reads before every single message, invisible in the chat itself. Paste ten of your own past posts in there with the instruction “write like this”. Every draft from then on starts in your voice instead of generic AI voice. Mine has explicit rules in it: no em dashes, no “leverage”, no “delve”. A local model will follow those rules. Translation: Interface strings, an email to a client in another language, subtitles. Fast, free and repeatable, so you can run a hundred of them. Transcript to draft: Record a call or a talk, feed the transcript in, get a structured draft back. This is a huge time saver in my week. Boring text surgery: Rename 200 layers to a consistent scheme, clean up a CSV, rewrite alt text for a folder of images, turn messy notes into a table. Anything you would not paste into a cloud tool: A contract, a salary conversation, an NDA’d brief, a medical letter. Whole industries cannot legally send data to a third party API. This is the only way they get to use AI at all. Working offline: Flights, trains, bad wifi. And what it is bad at: Current events. A model is trained at a point in time and has no internet of its own, so it knows nothing that happened after that day. Exact maths is the second one. And very long documents, which is a memory limit rather than a lack of intelligence. What you get and what you give up What you get Privacy: Nothing leaves your machine. Client contracts, salary discussions, an NDA’d brief, medical or legal documents: all fine, because there is no server involved. No bill per use: After the download every question is free. Run it all day and the cost is electricity. It works offline: On a plane, on a train, in a conference basement with bad wifi. Nobody can change it under you: No deprecation email, no new version that suddenly writes differently, no rate limit at the worst moment. You can point it at your own stuff: Attach a document and ask questions about it, entirely offline. What you give up A notch of quality: The best cloud models are still smarter. For most everyday work you will not notice, on hard reasoning you will. Your fans: A big model working hard heats your laptop and drains the battery. Disk space: Expect 8 to 24 GB per model. Memory pressure: The model sits in RAM the whole time it is loaded. Long documents cost extra memory on top. No web access by default: It knows nothing about today unless you give it tools. Nothing here is an either-or. Keep your cloud model subscription and let the local model take some of your routine work. This is the manual route, and it is worth doing once so you understand what is on your machine. If you would rather skip it, there is a prompt at the bottom of this post that hands the whole job to Claude. Step 1: Check what your Mac can handle This is the only technical decision in the whole guide. It comes down to memory. You need an Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or newer) on macOS 14 or later . Intel Macs are not supported. On Windows you need 16 GB RAM and a GPU with at least 4 GB VRAM ( system requirements ). First, what the B means. Gemma 4 12B is twelve billion parameters. Parameters are the internal dials the model was trained with. They are the only spec number these things really have. More dials means a better model, a bigger file and more memory. That is the whole trade you are making. The rule: the model file has to fit in your RAM with room left over for macOS and whatever else you have open. Leave roughly a third of your memory free and you will be fine. 8 GB : Gemma 3 4B, 3.3 GB download. Basic, but it runs 16 GB : Gemma 4 12B, 7.6 GB. The sweet spot for most people 24 GB : Qwen 3.6 27B, 17 GB. Close Figma while it works 32 GB : Qwen 3.6 35B, 22 GB. Best all-round, what I use 48 GB and up : the same Qwen 3.6 35B, but with the context window opened right up and a second small model loaded next to it. More memory buys you room to work, not a smarter model If you are on 16 GB, Gemma 4 12B is the one to get. It is small, writes clean prose and handles a 256K context window. If you are on 32 GB or more, Qwen 3.6 35B is the best all-round model most people can run. It is what I use every day. These are examples, not the only choice. New open models land every month. Gemma and Qwen carry this guide because they are the two families that currently sit in the size a Mac can actually run, and because I have used both. DeepSeek, Llama and plenty of others live in the same library. The names in this guide will move on. The memory maths will not, so learn that part and swap the names for whatever is current when you read it. Step 2: Install LM Studio LM Studio is a normal Mac app. It has a model browser, a chat window and a settings panel. It hides the machinery underneath. Download it, drag it to Applications, open it. That is the whole install. On Apple Silicon it runs models through Apple’s MLX, which is Apple’s own framework for running this kind of thing on the graphics chip. You do not have to do anything for that, it just means models run noticeably faster on a Mac than the numbers you see quoted for PCs. Step 3: Download your first model Click the Model Search icon, the magnifying glass over a little robot, last of the four icons in the narrow strip down the left edge. A search panel opens with a field at the top and a list of staff picks below it. Type the model name in. Pick a model and the right half of the panel fills with its details. Under Download Options the same model shows up several times over in different file sizes, with names like Q4 , Q4_K_M , Q8 and sometimes MLX . That is compression. It is the one piece of jargon worth learning. Think of an export dialog. The same picture leaves Figma as a 24 MB PNG or as a 2 MB JPEG at 80 percent and nobody in the review notices the difference. Model files work the same way. For Gemma 3 12B: the uncompressed file is 24 GB, Q8 is 13 GB, Q4 is 8.1 GB. Same model, three file sizes. The quality gap between them is far smaller than the size gap. Gemma 3 12B is just the example here. Every model on the shelf ships in the same set of sizes, so the same choice comes back every time you download one. Why 4-bit is what everyone takes: What you are short of is memory, not quality. Every gigabyte you spend on a less compressed file is a gigabyte you cannot spend on a better model. Gemma 3 12B at Q8 costs you 13 GB. For four gigabytes more you can run Qwen 3.6 27B at 4-bit instead, which is more than twice the model. That trade is why 4-bit ships as the default and why LM Studio tells you to take 4-bit or higher. MLX is not a compression level, it is Apple’s own format. Same model, built to run on the graphics chip of an Apple Silicon Mac. On a Mac, take it. Take the 4-bit version. If you see an MLX build of it, take that one. What if you have more memory than you need? On a 48 or 64 GB Mac the answer is still not a bigger file of the same model. Spend the extra memory on the three things that actually help: A longer context window. This is what runs out in real work: a sixty page PDF, a full call transcript, a long chat. Going from 32K to 256K costs memory and nothing else. A bigger model, if one exists. Today the useful local range tops out around 35B. That will change. Two models loaded at once. A small fast one for quick rewrites, a big one for the work that matters, no waiting for a swap. On 64 GB you can run the largest model in this guide at its full 256K context and still have Figma open. Download sizes are for the 4-bit versions, so a 16 GB Mac downloading Gemma 4 12B is pulling 7.6 GB. Grab a coffee. One badge worth knowing. If LM Studio shows a green Full GPU Offload Possible next to the download, the whole model fits in the memory your graphics chip can reach, which is where the speed comes from. Without that badge it still runs, just slower. Step 4: Your first conversation Go back to the chat tab, click Select a model to load at the top of the window (or press ⌘L ), pick what you downloaded and type something. The first message takes a few seconds longer because the model is being loaded into memory. Two settings worth touching, both in the model panel on the right: Context length. Everything the model can see at once: your standing instructions, the conversation so far and any document you dropped in. It is measured in tokens. 32K is roughly 24,000 words, call it a fifty page document. When it fills up the oldest part drops out of view, which is exactly why a model starts forgetting the beginning of a long chat. It eats RAM, so it usually defaults low. I run mine at 32K. If your Mac slows to a crawl, this is the first number to bring back down. Reasoning. Some models pause to think for 10 to 30 seconds before answering. That is normal, not a hang. If you find it annoying for everyday writing, switch reasoning off in the same panel. You can also drag a document into the chat and ask questions about it. That happens locally too, nothing gets uploaded. And what a token is, since the number is about to show up. Models read and write in tokens rather than words. A token is roughly three quarters of a word in English, so “design system” is two of them and something like “internationalisation” is four or five. Speed is counted in tokens per second. At 26 per second the text appears slightly faster than you can read it. Speed, from my own machine (M4 Max, Qwen 3.6 35B, 4-bit MLX, about 26 tokens per second): Short chat answer: 2 to 4 seconds A LinkedIn post: 4 to 8 seconds A newsletter with subject and body: 8 to 15 seconds A blog draft from a one hour call transcript: 60 to 120 seconds Step 5: Optional, the terminal route If you are comfortable in a terminal, Ollama does the same job with one command per model and no window to keep open. ollama run gemma4:12b downloads and starts it. Same models, less clicking. This is also where it stops being a chat window and starts being a tool. My own setup runs LM Studio as a local server. Small scripts point at it: one writes LinkedIn posts, one writes newsletters, one turns a transcript into a blog draft. Each is a text file with a system prompt in it. No subscription, no browser tab. 🤖 Or let Claude do the whole thing Everything above, done for you. This needs Claude Code, the version of Claude that can use your terminal, rather than the chat window. Paste this in and let it work: Set up a local LLM on this Mac for me. I am a designer, so explain what you are doing in plain language and do not ask me to run commands myself. Step 1: Check the machine first. How much memory it has, which chip, which macOS version. Tell me what you found. Step 2: Pick the model that fits. 8 GB: Gemma 3 4B. 16 GB: Gemma 4 12B. 24 GB: Qwen 3.6 27B. 32 GB and up: Qwen 3.6 35B. Always the 4-bit build, and the MLX build if there is one. Leave about a third of my memory free. Step 3: Install LM Studio if it is not there yet, plus its command line tool. Step 4: Download the model you picked. Tell me how big the download is before you start it. Step 5: Load it with a 32K context window and start the local server. Step 6: Prove it works. Ask it one question, show me the answer and the speed in tokens per second. Step 7: Finish with three lines. Which model I now have, how to start it again after a reboot, how to stop it when the fans get loud. If something fails, tell me what failed and what you would try next. Do not retry silently. The order matters. It checks the machine before it picks anything, so it cannot download a model that does not fit. Everything it installs is the same as above: LM Studio, one model file, nothing hidden. 🧭 A note on picking models later Model names move fast and most of what you read is out of date. Two things stay true. Check the date on any list you read, including this one. Every model above was checked on Ollama in August 2026. And ignore the headline releases. The models everyone writes about this summer are 300 billion parameters and up. They do not run on a laptop and they are not for you. The interesting work for local use is happening in the 12B to 35B range. Llama, the name most people still reach for, has not shipped anything that size in a year. 🚀 Start here Download LM Studio Model Search, look for Gemma 4 12B if you have 16 GB, Qwen 3.6 35B if you have 32 GB or more Take the 4-bit MLX version Set context length to 32K Paste ten of your own posts into the system prompt and ask it for a draft If you get stuck on any of the five, the Into Design Systems Slack is the fastest place to ask. Happy agentic coding! Sil Bormüller Into Design Systems + AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

graphicDesign.title: Designer Portraits: Susan Kare ⌘ The woman who gave the computer a face
graphicDesign.description: Good design is not about what medium you are working in. It’s about thinking hard about what you want to do and what you have to work with before you start. — SK Susan Kare joined Apple in 1982 as the sole creator of screen graphics in the Macintosh group. As the designer “ who gave the Macintosh a smile ” she is best known for developing the distinctive icons, typefaces, and other pixel elements that gave the Macintosh its characteristic look and feel. A sculptor picks up graph paper In 1982, Susan Kare was living in the Bay Area, welding a life-size razorback hog for a museum in Hot Springs, Arkansas. Her father, Morley Richard Kare, had founded the Monell Chemical Senses Center in Philadelphia, spending his career studying taste and smell. His daughter had a PhD from NYU, a background in sculpture and fine art, and zero experience with computers. Then Andy Hertzfeld called. Hertzfeld and Kare had known each other since they were fourteen, classmates at Harriton High School outside Philadelphia. He was now the lead software architect on a secret project at Apple: the Macintosh. He needed someone to design the icons and typefaces for its screen. He told her if she got some graph paper, she could make small images. Kare went to the University Art supply store in Palo Alto and bought a $2.50 sketchbook. That sketchbook now sits in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Susan Kare. Apple Macintosh OS icon sketchbook. 1982 — MoMa She went to the Palo Alto public library, checked out every book she could find on typography, and brought them to the interview to prove she knew something about type. “I went into it totally green” she said later. Apple offered her a fixed-length contract to design fonts and icons. In January 1983, she started working at Apple. Her business card read “Macintosh Artist.” Susan Kare, Apple's “Macintosh Artist” relaxes at her desk in 1984. Photographer: Norman Seeff 1,024 squares The Macintosh used a bit-mapped display. The display controlled every pixel on screen. Kare’s canvas was a 32-by-32 pixel grid. 1,024 squares to communicate a single idea. She understood the constraint immediately. “Bitmap graphics are like mosaics and needlepoint and other pseudo-digital art forms, all of which I had practiced before going to Apple,” she said. “I didn’t have any computer experience, but I had experience in graphic design.” No icon editor existed when she started. She learned to calculate the hex equivalent of her pixel drawings so Hertzfeld could keyboard them into the prototype. He built her a proper editor that generated hex values under the icons. Eventually she used MacPaint itself to create icons. A MacPaint screenshot featuring Kare’s artistry, 1983. Notice the icon menu at left and the Chicago system font used for the pull-down menus. Some icons already existed from the Lisa, Apple’s earlier computer. The arrow cursor. The document with a folded corner. The trash can. The Lisa’s interface was functional but clinical, icons designed by engineers to label functions, not to invite use. It also used non-square pixels, so every element needed reworking for the Mac’s display. Kare refined the trash can. She created the application icon, a hand holding a pencil against a diamond shape, to distinguish apps from documents. She designed the Happy Mac, the smiling face that greeted users at startup. She designed the ticking bomb that appeared during system failures. For the copy function, she tried drawing a photocopier. Then she drew a cat looking in a mirror. Copy cat. She scrapped it because it wouldn’t translate internationally. The lasso, the paint bucket, the paintbrush. Each icon went through rounds of sketching on graph paper before touching a screen. Her process was the same as any visual designer working in any medium in any century. Pencil, paper, iteration. The screen was just the final surface. Kare's Happy Macintosh icon appeared at startup, greeting users with a smile to let them know everything was okay. She designed warmth into a machine. Fonts in 9 by 7 dots Most digital typefaces in 1983 were monospaced. Every character occupied the same width. Kare wanted proportional fonts, letters that breathed according to their natural shape. Each letter had to fit in a grid of 9 by 7 dots. The bold system font started as “Elefont.” It became Chicago, the typeface that would appear on the Macintosh and later the iPod for over twenty years. Kare and Hertzfeld named the early fonts after commuter train stops on Philadelphia’s Main Line: Overbrook, Merion, Ardmore, Rosemont, Paoli. Steve Jobs told them the names were too parochial. He wanted world-class cities. The fonts became New York, Geneva, London, Toronto, Venice. One font, Ransom, looked like cutout letters from a kidnapper’s note. Jobs renamed it San Francisco. Another, Cairo, featured tiny pictograms: a palm tree, a crescent moon, a skateboard. Decades before Apple introduced emoji, Kare had already drawn proto-emojis into a font. The command key and the Swedish campground ⌘ Every keyboard needs a modifier key. The Mac team struggled to find the right symbol for theirs. Kare found the answer in Henry Dreyfuss’s Symbol Sourcebook, a reference she kept at her desk at Apple. The symbol marked interesting features on Swedish campgrounds. It was abstract enough to work as a keyboard glyph, meaningful enough to carry intention. It became ⌘, one of the most recognized symbols in computing. The pirate flag Steve Jobs liked to tell the Mac team: “ It’s better to be a pirate than join the navy. ” When the team moved into a new building, Bandley 3 , programmer Steve Capps wanted a flag. He asked Kare to design one. She drew a Jolly Roger with the eyepatch replaced by Apple’s rainbow logo. They flew it over the entrance. It stayed there for over a year. At one point, the Lisa team stole it. In 2016, Apple flew the flag again to mark the company’s 40th anniversary. This wallpape r is a nod to the Jolly Roger that flew over Bandley 3 in 1983, the building the Mac team worked in as they put the finishing touches on the Macintosh. Apple recently flew a recreation of the original 1983 flag in 2016 , when it celebrated its 40th anniversary on April 1st, shortly before moving its HQ from Infinite Loop to Apple Park. And the flag is still available on Susan Kare's website . After the Mac The Macintosh shipped in January 1984. The entire visual language Kare created came from roughly one year of work. When Steve Jobs left Apple in 1985, Kare followed him to NeXT as creative director. She was one of the company’s first ten employees. At NeXT, she connected Jobs with one of her design heroes. Kare was a devoted Paul Rand fan. She introduced Jobs to Rand’s books, and together they hired Rand to design the NeXT logo. Kare and David Kelley visited Rand at his studio. Rand, then in his seventies, told them: “I’ve been doing this for fifty-five years, and I know what you should do.” Susan Kare, center, was a creative director at NeXT, and she left with Jobs after his ouster at Apple. Kim Jenkins, right, was a key member of the NeXT marketing team. Kare founded her own studio, Susan Kare LLP, in 1989. Over the next three decades, she designed interface elements for Microsoft, Oracle, Facebook, IBM, and Sony Pictures. She designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. In 2003, she served on the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee, designing coins for the United States Mint. In 2015, she joined Pinterest as product design lead. In 2018, AIGA awarded her the AIGA Medal, one of the profession’s highest honors. Kare designed the card deck for Windows Solitaire, arguably her most-seen work, viewed by hundreds of millions of people who never knew her name. The proof of concept The Museum of Modern Art calls Kare “a pioneering and influential computer iconographer.” The label misses the point. She made the Macintosh feel human and had never touched a computer before Apple hired her. She came from sculpture, fine art, mosaics, needlepoint. She treated the pixel grid the same way she treated any design surface: as a constraint that shapes the work. “I hoped to help counter the stereotypical image of computers as cold and intimidating,” Kare said. Someone with a $2.50 sketchbook and a sculptor’s eye decided that the visual language of technology should borrow from the one humans already knew. That turned out to be enough. “I still spend my days turning dots on and off.” Today, Kare is working as a design architect at Niantic Labs and still runs her own studio in San Francisco. She sells limited-edition signed prints of her icon work, collaborates with brands like Ledger on pixel art for hardware , and her original 1982 sketchbooks remain on display at MoMA. Needlepoint to Ledger Nano™: A Conversation with Susan Kare Apple turns 50 this year. ( 50 years of thinking different. ) Researching Susan Kare felt like walking back to where it all started; reading about how she approached design problems, how she collaborated, how she used constraints to shape the work.
